title: Graphene-based materials for energy storage: a review of synthesis, properties, and applications
abstract: Abstract Graphene-based materials have emerged as transformative candidates for energy storage systems, effectively addressing limitations such as low energy density, poor stability, and limited scalability in conventional technologies. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of the synthesis techniques, structural properties, and diverse applications of graphene in advanced energy storage devices, including supercapacitors (SCs), lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), sodium-ion batteries (SIBs), and hybrid systems. Key synthesis approaches such as chemical vapor deposition (CVD), chemical reduction of graphene oxide (GO), and biomass-derived graphene are discussed as promising sustainable alternatives. Furthermore, this review highlights recent advancements in next-generation hybrid graphene architectures that have resulted in a 30–50% enhancement in energy storage performance compared to conventional materials. Challenges such as synthesis scalability, long-term stability, and compatibility with existing technologies are discussed, alongside future directions to enable widespread commercialization. Real-world case studies illustrate the transformative potential of graphene-based energy storage technologies, bridging the gap between laboratory innovations and large-scale deployment. This review serves as a critical resource for researchers, policymakers, and industry stakeholders, providing insights into the pathways for sustainable and high-performance energy storage solutions.
journal: Journal of Materials Science: Materials in Energy

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Advanced energy storage systems are vital given the growing need for sustainable energy solutions worldwide, which is being fueled by the switch to renewable energy, electric vehicles, and portable electronics. Current technologies such as LIBs, SIBs, and SCs face significant challenges, including limited energy densities, short cycle lives, slow charge/discharge rates, and environmental concerns related to material sourcing [ 1 ]. These limitations highlight the necessity for innovative materials to improve energy storage performance while ensuring sustainability and scalability. In the field of energy storage, graphene, a two-dimensional material composed of a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a honeycomb lattice, has garnered a lot of attention due to its exceptional properties [ 2 ]. Its ultra-high surface area, superior electrical conductivity, exceptional mechanical strength, and chemical stability make it a promising material to address the challenges faced by conventional technologies. Moreover, graphene’s adaptability allows it to be integrated with a wide range of metal oxides, polymers, and nanostructures, opening the door for notable improvements in the functionality of energy storage devices. Because of their distinct structural and electrochemical characteristics, graphene and its derivatives are ideal for a wide range of energy conversion and storage applications [ 3 ]. Depending on their size, morphology, and surface functionalization, graphene materials can be tailored for specific roles in SCs, LIBs, and other energy devices. As illustrated in Fig.  1 , graphene-based materials can be categorized based on their dimensions and functionalities, highlighting their applicability in different energy storage and conversion technologies. Graphene-based materials offer distinct advantages over conventional energy storage materials, making them highly suitable for enhancing the efficiency and performance of devices such as SCs, LIBs, and SIBs. Unlike activated carbon, which has limited electrochemical active sites and suffers from poor rate performance, graphene’s large surface area provides abundant active sites for ion adsorption and rapid charge storage, enabling higher capacitance and faster charge/discharge rates. Similarly, compared to transition metal oxides (TMOs), which often suffer from volume expansion during cycling, graphene exhibits exceptional mechanical strength and structural stability, ensuring better cyclic performance and longer device lifespan. Furthermore, silicon-based anodes in LIBs, while offering high capacity, undergo significant volume changes during lithiation and delithiation, leading to structural degradation and capacity loss [ 5 ]. In contrast, graphene-based anodes mitigate these issues by accommodating volume expansion, providing enhanced mechanical flexibility, and maintaining structural integrity over prolonged cycling. Moreover, graphene’s superior electrical conductivity significantly outperforms other carbonaceous materials, allowing for rapid electron transport and minimizing internal resistance, which is essential for achieving high power density and improved efficiency. These attributes, combined with graphene’s chemical tunability and ease of functionalization, enable the development of hybrid structures that synergistically combine the benefits of graphene with other materials, addressing the limitations of traditional energy storage technologies.

Several previous reviews have explored graphene’s potential for energy storage. Zhu et al. provided foundational insights into graphene-based materials, focusing on their application in LIBs and SCs [ 6 ], while Liu et al. examined broader energy applications of graphene, including its use in fuel cells and hydrogen storage [ 7 ]. Lv et al. further discussed the electrochemical opportunities and challenges of graphene, emphasizing its role in enhancing battery performance [ 8 ]. More recent works, such as Fan et al., focused on 3D graphene-based materials for energy storage, highlighting their improved structural stability and enhanced ion transport [ 9 ]. Similarly, Jiang et al. examined how three-dimensional printing methods for graphene-based materials affect energy conversion and storage, demonstrating improvements in structural optimization and device construction [ 10 ]. Existing reviews often do not address the challenges of  scalability, environmental impact, and cost-effectiveness  of graphene production. Moreover, the integration of graphene with hybrid materials and its application in  next-generation flexible devices  remains underexplored. This review specifically targets these knowledge gaps to provide a holistic understanding of graphene’s potential in real-world energy storage applications.

In contrast, recent studies by Togun et al. and Abdulrazzaq et al. have focused on phase change materials (PCMs) and thermal energy storage (TES) systems. Togun et al. reviewed hybrid enhancement techniques for PCM-based heat exchangers, focusing on improving heat transfer performance in thermal systems. They reported that using hybrid PCM systems improved heat transfer efficiency, with notable improvements in thermal conductivity and melting rates [ 11 ]. Abdulrazzaq et al. explored the impact of curved fins on the performance of shell-and-tube latent heat storage systems, where curved fins resulted in faster melting rates and improved heat transfer uniformity [ 12 ]. Sultan et al. investigated innovative undulated PCM containers in shell-and-tube TES systems, highlighting improvements in discharge performance due to optimized container geometry [ 13 ]. Similarly, Nandi et al. examined the energy efficiency of nano-enhanced PCMs (NePCM) using graphene, Al₂O₃, and CuO, demonstrating improvements in thermal conductivity and energy storage capacity [ 14 ]. Khedher et al. modified the geometry of PCM containers in TES systems to enhance melting dynamics, achieving faster melting rates with modified geometries [ 15 ]. Nandi et al. further demonstrated improved melting performance in PCM systems by incorporating modified fins and nanoparticles under solar irradiation, resulting in enhanced thermal performance and reduced melting time [ 16 ]. While these PCM-focused studies have significantly advanced the understanding of thermal energy storage, they remain distinct from the electrochemical energy storage focus of this review. Unlike these works, which emphasize heat transfer efficiency and thermal management, this review provides a comprehensive analysis of graphene-based materials in electrochemical energy storage applications, including LIBs, SIBs, and SCs. Furthermore, this review extends beyond material performance by addressing critical aspects such as sustainable and scalable synthesis methods, hybrid material integration for synergistic effects, and economic feasibility considerations for real-world commercialization. By bridging these knowledge gaps, this review advances the current state-of-the-art in graphene-based energy storage technologies and provides a roadmap for future research and innovation.

While several reviews have addressed graphene-based materials for energy storage, most are typically focused on specific aspects such as synthesis techniques, material properties, or individual device applications. This review aims to provide a more integrated discussion by covering multiple interconnected aspects of graphene research for energy storage systems. Specifically, it highlights recent advances in scalable and sustainable synthesis strategies, including green chemistry approaches and biomass-derived routes, with an emphasis on their potential for industrial translation. In addition, the review discusses the role of graphene-based hybrid and heterostructured materials in improving electrochemical performance through synergistic effects. Emerging applications in flexible and wearable energy storage devices are also considered, reflecting the evolving demand for lightweight and mechanically adaptable systems.

sections.heading: Synthesis of graphene-based Materials
paragraphs: The synthesis of graphene-based materials significantly influences their structural, electrical, and electrochemical properties, thereby impacting their performance in energy storage applications. Various synthesis techniques have been developed, broadly classified into chemical, mechanical, and electrochemical methods. Each approach presents unique advantages and challenges in terms of scalability, cost-effectiveness, and material quality. Researchers have actively worked on optimizing these methods to overcome existing limitations and enhance graphene’s suitability for energy storage applications.

Chemical processes that produce high-quality graphene with regulated thickness and purity include chemical vapor deposition (CVD) and chemical reduction of graphene oxide (GO). CVD remains the preferred method for fabricating monolayer graphene with exceptional electrical conductivity, making it highly suitable for SCs and LIBs. However, CVD requires high temperatures and expensive catalysts, limiting its scalability. To mitigate these issues, researchers have developed low-temperature CVD processes and alternative catalyst materials like copper foils with optimized grain structures, which reduce production costs while maintaining graphene quality [ 17 ]. Meanwhile, chemical reduction of GO provides a scalable approach for producing reduced graphene oxide (rGO) with tunable functional groups, but incomplete reduction leads to residual oxygen-containing defects that affect conductivity. Advanced reduction techniques, such as hydrothermal reduction and plasma-assisted reduction, have been introduced to improve the removal of oxygen groups while preserving graphene’s structure [ 18 ]. Mechanical methods, including liquid-phase exfoliation and ball milling, offer scalable and cost-effective ways to produce graphene nanosheets. Liquid-phase exfoliation involves dispersing graphite in solvents followed by ultrasonication, but the process often results in low exfoliation efficiency and small flake sizes [ 19 ]. To address these drawbacks, optimized surfactants and solvent mixtures, such as N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) and isopropanol blends, have been employed to improve exfoliation yield and prevent restacking of graphene sheets. Ball milling, another promising method, suffers from uncontrolled defect formation due to mechanical forces [ 20 ]. To counter this, researchers have optimized milling speed, duration, and inert gas environments to minimize structural damage while maintaining high exfoliation efficiency. However, one major challenge is the non-uniform exfoliation, which leads to variations in flake size and thickness. To overcome this, precise control of applied voltage and electrolyte composition has been implemented to achieve consistent exfoliation. Additionally, the introduction of buffering agents and optimized anions has improved the exfoliation rate while reducing oxidative damage to graphene sheets. sections.heading: Chemical vapor deposition (CVD)
paragraphs: CVD is one of the most widely utilized methods for the high-quality synthesis of graphene, offering significant advantages in producing large-area, continuous graphene films with controlled thickness and structural integrity. The mechanical strength, electrical conductivity, and transparency of graphene may be precisely controlled via CVD, in contrast to other synthesis methods. These characteristics are essential for a variety of innovative applications, such as energy conversion and storage devices.

Methane (CH₄), ethylene (C₂H₄), or acetylene (C₂H₂) are examples of carbon-containing precursor gases that are delivered into a high-temperature reaction chamber, usually heated to temperatures between 800 °C and 1000°C, in the CVD process. This precursor gas is decomposed by the heat and forms carbon atoms, which then deposit onto a substrate, commonly copper (Cu) or nickel (Ni), resulting in the formation of a graphene layer. The choice of substrate is critical as it influences the quality and number of graphene layers, with copper being a preferred choice due to its low catalytic activity for carbon atoms, allowing for the growth of monolayer graphene. The process begins with the cleaning of the substrate to remove any contaminants and oxidation layers. Once the substrate is prepared, the carbon precursor is introduced into the reaction chamber, where it undergoes thermal decomposition. The carbon atoms are then deposited onto the substrate’s surface, where they self-assemble into a graphene lattice [ 21 ]. The substrate acts as both a catalyst for the decomposition of the precursor and as a support for the growing graphene layer. The process is conducted under a controlled atmosphere, often with a flow of inert gases such as hydrogen (H₂) or argon (Ar), to avoid oxidation and facilitate the reduction of oxygenated species from the graphene surface.

One of the significant advantages of CVD is its ability to produce high-quality graphene with minimal defects and impurities. The method is capable of creating monolayer or bilayer graphene films with large surface areas, which are essential for applications in energy storage devices such as SCs, LIBs, and fuel cells [ 22 ]. The enhanced electrical conductivity and charge mobility of CVD-grown graphene are a result of its large domain size and good crystalline purity, making it highly suitable for energy-related applications. The quality of graphene synthesized via CVD is strongly influenced by process parameters such as temperature, pressure, and gas flow rate. Higher temperatures (≈950–1000°C) and controlled low-pressure conditions favor the growth of uniform, monolayer graphene with minimal defects, while lower temperatures or higher pressures often lead to multilayer formation. The H₂/CH₄ ratio also plays a vital role—higher hydrogen concentrations promote cleaner, smoother films by controlling carbon deposition. Optimizing these parameters ensures precise control over graphene’s layer number, crystallinity, and conductivity, enabling consistent production of high-quality graphene for energy storage applications.

However, the CVD method does come with several challenges that limit its scalability and cost-effectiveness. Although CVD produces high-quality graphene on catalytic metal substrates, the quality of the final usable film is often affected by post-growth transfer processes required for device integration. One of the primary challenges is the high temperature required for the process, which limits the choice of substrates to those that can withstand such temperatures, such as copper and nickel. While copper is often used for its excellent graphene growth properties, it is expensive and can also suffer from contamination during the transfer of graphene to other substrates, further complicating the process [ 23 ]. Another limitation is the relatively slow growth rate of graphene, which can result in long processing times for producing large-area graphene films. Moreover, the transfer process—where the graphene grown on the metallic substrate is moved onto a desired insulating or flexible substrate for device integration—introduces additional challenges. The transfer procedure typically involves etching away the metal catalyst, which can lead to defects in the graphene layer, compromising its mechanical and electrical properties [ 24 ]. To address these issues, researchers have explored alternative strategies, such as directly growing graphene on insulating substrates like silicon carbide (SiC), which does not require transfer and results in high-quality graphene films. Another promising direction is the development of continuous and roll-to-roll CVD techniques, which could potentially allow for scalable production of high-quality graphene at reduced costs. In addition to these challenges, the uniformity of the graphene layer is another crucial factor that impacts its performance in energy storage devices. While CVD can produce large-area graphene films, the uniformity in terms of thickness and morphology can vary, especially when scaling up the process [ 17 ]. Variations in the growth rate, precursor flow, and temperature distribution within the reaction chamber can lead to inconsistencies in the quality of the graphene produced. To mitigate this, advancements in reactor design and process optimization have been pursued, including the use of more sophisticated precursor gases, better control over reaction parameters, and the introduction of additional gases like hydrogen to promote uniformity during growth.

Recent advancements have focused on improving the scalability of CVD for large-area graphene production while maintaining high quality. For instance, the use of low-cost, scalable substrates like copper foils and flexible materials is being explored to reduce costs. Additionally, optimization of the precursor gases and their concentrations, as well as the introduction of novel plasma-enhanced CVD techniques, has been shown to enhance the growth rate and quality of the graphene films. These developments are key to overcoming the limitations of traditional CVD methods and making graphene a viable material for large-scale, industrial applications, particularly in energy storage technologies.

sections.heading: Chemical reduction of graphene oxide (GO)
paragraphs: The chemical reduction of GO is a widely utilized method for synthesizing rGO, which demonstrates improved qualities like heat stability, electrical conductivity and mechanical strength. Oxygen-containing functional groups such as carboxyl, epoxy, and hydroxyl groups are added to the graphene sheets to create GO. These groups impart hydrophilicity to GO, making it dispersible in water and suitable for various applications. However, these oxygenated functional groups are detrimental to the electronic properties of GO. The chemical reduction process aims to remove some of these groups, restoring the electrical conductivity and other desirable properties of graphene.

The synthesis of rGO from GO involves exposing GO to reducing agents, which donate electrons to the oxygenated groups on the graphene sheets, facilitating their removal. This results in the restoration of conjugated π-bonding, characteristic of the graphene structure. The reduction process is typically carried out in an aqueous or organic solvent, and the reducing agents commonly used include hydrazine (N₂H₄), sodium borohydride (NaBH₄), ascorbic acid, and even plant extracts or polyphenols as greener alternatives. The reduction reaction can occur under various conditions of temperature, solvent concentration, and reaction time. The synthesis process begins with the preparation of GO, typically using the Hummers’ method or its modifications, which entail applying potent oxidizing chemicals, such as concentrated sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) and potassium permanganate (KMnO₄), to graphite. This process results in the introduction of functional groups on the graphene surface, making it hydrophilic and dispersible in solvents. Following the production of GO, chemical reduction is carried out by introducing reducing agents, which remove the oxygen groups and restore the graphene network. The general reaction for this reduction is the interaction of GO with the reducing agent, leading to the formation of rGO and the release of reduced oxygen groups such as water (H₂O) or carbon dioxide (CO₂) [ 25 ]. After reduction, rGO is typically washed to remove any residual reducing agents and by-products, followed by drying and sometimes thermal annealing under an inert atmosphere to further improve its properties.

Despite its widespread use, several challenges are associated with the chemical reduction of GO. One of the major issues is incomplete reduction, where not all oxygen groups are eliminated, leaving rGO with some of its oxygen capabilities intact. The material’s electrical conductivity is impacted by this partial reduction and overall performance, particularly in applications that require high conductivity, such as energy storage devices. Another challenge lies in the use of toxic and hazardous reducing agents, such as hydrazine, which present safety and environmental concerns. Furthermore, the reduction process can introduce defects into the graphene structure, which may impair the material’s mechanical properties and conductivity. To address these challenges, researchers have proposed several advancements in the chemical reduction process [ 26 ]. One solution to the issue of incomplete reduction is the use of milder reducing agents and optimized reaction conditions. For instance, the use of greener, more environmentally friendly reducing agents, such as plant extracts or natural polymers, has gained attention. These green reducing agents are not only safer but can also provide more controlled reduction of GO while preserving certain functional groups that may be beneficial for specific applications, such as enhancing dispersion in composites or improving electrochemical properties. Moreover, optimizing the reaction temperature, time, and concentration of the reducing agent has been shown to yield rGO with fewer defects and improved properties. Another strategy for overcoming the challenges of chemical reduction is the application of post-reduction treatments, such as thermal annealing. By heating the rGO under an inert atmosphere (e.g., nitrogen or hydrogen), the residual oxygen groups can be further eliminated, and the graphene structure can be further enhanced. Additionally, electrochemical reduction has emerged as an alternative to chemical reduction [ 27 ]. This method involves applying a current to GO in an electrolyte solution, which can provide more control over the reduction process, leading to higher-quality rGO with fewer defects and better electrical conductivity.

While, the chemical reduction of GO remains one of the most accessible and scalable methods for synthesizing rGO, it is not without its challenges. These challenges, including incomplete reduction, the toxicity of reducing agents, and the introduction of defects, hinder the full realization of rGO’s potential. However, advancements such as the use of green reducing agents, optimized reaction conditions, and post-treatment techniques like thermal annealing and electrochemical reduction offer promising solutions to these issues. By improving these techniques, GO may be chemically reduced more effectively and sustainably, producing high-quality rGO that can be used in a variety of applications, especially energy storage devices.

sections.heading: Mechanical and liquid-phase exfoliation
paragraphs: Mechanical and liquid-phase exfoliation techniques are widely explored for producing graphene and graphene-based materials on a larger scale, offering a cost-effective alternative to chemical synthesis methods. These techniques involve the separation of graphene layers from graphite or graphite oxide and can be employed for both high-quality monolayer graphene as well as functionalized graphene derivatives, which are crucial for various energy storage applications such as SCs, batteries, and fuel cells.

Mechanical Exfoliation is one of the simplest methods for producing graphene, especially at a small scale, and is commonly known for its use in isolating high-quality graphene. In this method, graphite is mechanically cleaved using an adhesive tape, a process famously called as the Scotch tape method. This technique is based on the principle of applying pressure to the graphite surface, which causes the individual graphene layers to detach [ 28 ]. The process involves repeated sticking and peeling of adhesive tape on a piece of highly oriented pyrolytic graphite (HOPG), which results in thin graphene layers that can be transferred to a substrate. The primary advantage of mechanical exfoliation is that it can produce high-quality, defect-free graphene with minimal functionalization. However, this technique is not easily scalable to industrial levels due to its low yield and reliance on manual handling, making it impractical for large-scale applications. On the other hand, Liquid-Phase Exfoliation is a more scalable method for producing graphene sheets from graphite, providing a promising route for the bulk production of graphene and GO [ 29 ]. In this process, graphite or graphite oxide is dispersed in a suitable solvent (e.g., H 2 O, ethanol, or NMP) and subjected to mechanical forces to break apart the graphite layers into graphene sheets. This can be achieved through sonication, high shear mixing, or using a stirring device to create high shear forces that help separate the graphene layers. Usually, ultrasonic treatment is used in the exfoliation process. High-frequency sound waves create cavitation bubbles in the liquid, which can disrupt the interlayer van der Waals forces between graphene sheets by creating localized high temperatures and pressures.

Both mechanical and liquid-phase exfoliation techniques offer significant potential for the scalable production of graphene. While mechanical exfoliation remains the method of choice for high-quality, small-scale production, liquid-phase exfoliation has become increasingly popular for large-scale graphene production due to its simplicity, scalability, and the ability to produce dispersions of graphene suitable for a wide range of applications. Despite the challenges in achieving consistent monolayer graphene with controlled properties, ongoing research into improving the exfoliation methods and post-processing techniques will likely enhance the quality, yield, and applicability of graphene for energy storage and other advanced technologies.

sections.heading: Hydrothermal and solvothermal methods
paragraphs: Hydrothermal and solvothermal methods are widely used for the synthesis of GO and rGO, which are essential materials for various energy storage applications. These methods involve the use of high-temperature and high-pressure conditions in an aqueous or organic solvent environment to facilitate the reduction and exfoliation of graphite-based precursors. Significant benefits are provided by the hydrothermal and solvothermal procedures in terms of scalability, material property control, and the production of superior graphene derivatives.

One of the most popular methods for creating GO and its reduced version, rGO, is the hydrothermal process. In this method, GO is first synthesized by oxidizing graphite with a strong oxidizing agent, such as KMnO₄ or sodium nitrate (NaNO₃), in a concentrated acid solution (usually H 2 SO 4 ). GO is created via the oxidation process, which adds oxygen-containing functional groups to the graphene sheets’ surface, including hydroxyl, carboxyl, and epoxide groups [ 30 ]. Once GO is prepared, it can be reduced to rGO using hydrothermal treatment. In a typical hydrothermal reduction process, a dispersion of GO is placed in a sealed autoclave with water or an organic solvent and heated to temperatures typically ranging from 150 °C to 250 °C. Under these high-pressure and high-temperature conditions, the oxygen-containing functional groups in GO are partially removed, and the GO sheets are restored to a rGO. The reduction process often involves the use of reducing agents such as hydrazine (N₂H₄), sodium borohydride (NaBH₄), or ascorbic acid. Alternatively, the heat and pressure in the hydrothermal environment itself may act as a driving force for the reduction, leading to the formation of rGO. The hydrothermal method offers several advantages [ 31 ]. It is highly scalable, cost-effective, and environmentally friendly since it typically uses water or low-toxicity solvents. Moreover, it allows for the precise control over the reduction degree of GO, which directly influences the electrical conductivity and structural properties of rGO. The process can also enhance the dispersion and exfoliation of graphene sheets, producing rGO that is more porous and has a larger surface area—a desirable property for energy storage devices like batteries and SCs. However, there are some challenges associated with the hydrothermal method. One of the main issues is the incomplete reduction of GO in some cases, which can lead to a mixture of partially rGO and residual oxygen-containing functional groups [ 32 ]. This can negatively affect the electrical conductivity and electrochemical performance of the resulting rGO. Additionally, the need for high-pressure reactors (autoclaves) and precise temperature control can increase the cost and complexity of the process. Furthermore, optimizing the reduction process for specific applications requires careful tuning of parameters such as temperature, pressure, reaction time, and the type of reducing agent used.

The solvothermal method is a variation of the hydrothermal approach in which an organic solvent (e.g., ethanol, ethylene glycol, or dimethylformamide) is used instead of water to aid the reduction and exfoliation of GO. Like the hydrothermal method, the solvothermal process involves placing GO in a sealed vessel (autoclave) with the solvent, followed by heating to high temperatures under controlled pressure [ 33 ]. The primary difference between hydrothermal and solvothermal methods is the use of organic solvents, which can offer enhanced solubility and stability for certain reactants, enabling better control over the reduction and exfoliation processes. In the solvothermal reduction of GO, the solvent plays a crucial role in facilitating the removal of oxygen functional groups. The solvothermal method often employs reducing agents such as hydrazine or sodium borohydride, similar to the hydrothermal reduction process. However, because the solvents used in solvothermal reactions are often more reactive than water, they can provide stronger reducing conditions, which can result in a higher degree of reduction of GO and thus the production of rGO with better electrical conductivity [ 34 ]. Solvothermal processes also have the advantage of enabling the synthesis of graphene-based nanomaterials with tailored properties, such as the controlled size, morphology, and surface characteristics of rGO. The ability to adjust the solvent and reducing agents in the solvothermal process allows for the synthesis of highly uniform rGO, which can be important for achieving consistent performance in energy storage applications. Additionally, solvothermal methods have been reported to produce rGO with enhanced dispersibility in non-aqueous solvents, making it easier to integrate into composites or inks for various applications [ 35 ]. Nevertheless, solvothermal methods face similar challenges as the hydrothermal method, such as the need for high-pressure equipment and precise control over experimental conditions. Moreover, the use of organic solvents and reducing agents can introduce additional safety concerns and environmental considerations. Some solvents used in solvothermal reactions may also have higher toxicity compared to water, which can complicate the sustainability of the process.

The properties of graphene obtained via hydrothermal or solvothermal routes are highly dependent on synthesis parameters such as  temperature, pressure, solvent type, reaction time, and reducing agent . Low temperatures yield incomplete reduction, while excessive heat causes sheet aggregation and defects. Reaction duration and solvent polarity influence reduction degree and sheet dispersion, creating a trade-off between conductivity and stability. Although chemical reducers like hydrazine improve conductivity, greener alternatives such as ascorbic acid are preferred for sustainability. Moreover, pressure and pH critically affect exfoliation and defect density, impacting ion transport and electrochemical behavior. Hence, precise optimization of these parameters is vital to achieve uniform, conductive, and reproducible graphene for energy applications. Both the hydrothermal and solvothermal methods provide excellent platforms for synthesizing high-quality GO and rGO, with the key distinction being the use of water versus organic solvents. The hydrothermal method is generally more environmentally friendly and cost-effective, especially when water is used as the solvent. It also offers better scalability for large-scale production. However, the solvothermal method offers more versatility, particularly in terms of the types of solvents that can be employed, allowing for enhanced control over the reduction process [ 36 ]. Both methods are widely used in the production of rGO for energy storage applications. The choice of method often depends on the specific requirements of the application, such as the desired degree of reduction, the need for a specific solvent or reducing agent, and scalability considerations. Both hydrothermal and solvothermal processes can be optimized to produce rGO being perfect candidates for energy storage devices like SCs, LIBs, and other energy conversion technologies because of their large surface area, strong electrical conductivity, and superior electrochemical performance.

sections.heading: Emerging synthesis techniques
paragraphs: The production of graphene and its derivatives has shifted in recent years toward environmentally benign and sustainable processes, especially with the usage of graphene obtained from biomass. Traditional methods such as CVD and chemical reduction of GO often rely on petrochemical-based feedstocks and harsh chemicals, which can have a significant environmental impact [ 37 ,  38 ]. To mitigate this, researchers have increasingly turned their attention to green chemistry and renewable resources, with biomass-derived graphene emerging as a promising alternative. This section explores the advantages, challenges, and advancements in the field of biomass-derived graphene and other sustainable synthesis methods, with a focus on their potential applications in energy storage technologies.

Biomass-derived graphene refers to graphene materials that are synthesized from renewable organic resources such as agricultural waste, wood, and other plant-based materials. The use of biomass as a precursor for graphene synthesis offers multiple advantages. First, biomass is widely available, inexpensive, and environmentally friendly, making it an attractive alternative to traditional fossil-fuel-derived feedstocks. Second, many biomass materials are rich in carbon, which can be converted into graphene through various processes, including pyrolysis and hydrothermal carbonization. By utilizing waste products from agriculture and forestry, the production of biomass-derived graphene also contributes to reducing environmental waste, making it a sustainable approach to producing advanced materials [ 39 ].

One of the most common methods used for producing biomass-derived graphene is pyrolysis, or thermal decomposition, where biomass materials are heated at high temperatures in the absence of oxygen. This process converts the carbon content of the biomass into carbon-rich materials, which can then be further processed into GO or rGO. Following pyrolysis, further chemical or thermal treatments can be applied to achieve graphene-like materials. Hydrothermal carbonization (HTC) is another technique used to convert biomass into graphene. In HTC, biomass is treated under high pressure and temperature in the presence of water, allowing for the conversion of the biomass into carbonaceous materials in a more controlled and environmentally friendly manner compared to pyrolysis [ 40 ]. Another promising development in the field of sustainable graphene synthesis is the electrochemical reduction of CO₂. This technique offers the dual benefit of reducing greenhouse gas emissions and producing valuable carbon-based materials, including graphene. By applying an electrical current to CO₂ in an appropriate electrolyte, carbon atoms are reduced and can form graphene-like materials. This method holds promise not only for producing graphene in a sustainable manner but also for contributing to the reduction of atmospheric CO₂ levels, thus aligning with global efforts to combat climate change [ 41 ]. In addition to CO₂ reduction, the use of green solvents in graphene synthesis is gaining traction. Green solvents, such as ionic liquids or supercritical CO₂, are an eco-friendly substitute for traditional solvents since they are non-toxic, biodegradable, and sourced from renewable resources. These solvents offer a more sustainable option for producing high-quality graphene, while also reducing the environmental and health risks associated with traditional chemicals used in graphene production.

Another innovative approach is the use of biological or biomimetic methods for synthesizing graphene. This involves utilizing microorganisms, such as bacteria, fungi, or algae, to produce graphene through natural processes. For example, certain bacteria can reduce GO into rGO under mild conditions, producing high-quality graphene without the need for harsh chemicals or extreme temperatures [ 42 ]. These biological methods are considered to be energy-efficient and environmentally friendly, with the potential for low-cost production of graphene at large scales. Photothermal reduction is another sustainable technique that utilizes sunlight or artificial light to drive the reduction of GO into rGO. This method leverages renewable energy sources, such as solar power, to induce the reduction reaction in GO suspensions, making it a cost-effective and energy-efficient approach to producing graphene materials.

Although biomass-derived graphene holds great potential, there are several challenges associated with its synthesis. One of the primary challenges is optimizing the quality and consistency of the resulting graphene material. The properties of biomass-derived graphene can vary depending on the type of biomass used, the particular processing parameters (temperature, pressure, and duration), as well as the post-treatment procedures used. For energy storage applications, the material must have a high surface area, good electrical conductivity, and stability [ 43 ]. To guarantee constant material quality, the synthesis procedures must be progressively improved. Another challenges remain in terms of scalability and material quality. For example, while biomass-derived graphene can be produced at a small scale using pyrolysis or hydrothermal methods, achieving consistent material properties and scaling up the production process is still a significant challenge. Researchers are exploring hybrid methods, combining different synthesis techniques or improving reaction conditions, to overcome these obstacles and make the production of high-quality, biomass-derived graphene feasible at industrial scales.

Quantitatively, biomass-derived graphene generally exhibits lower structural quality than CVD-grown graphene because of its heterogeneous carbon precursors and less controlled graphitization process. Typical CVD-grown graphene exhibits electrical conductivity on the order of 10 5  −10 6  S m − 1 , Raman ID/IG ratios below 0.1, indicating very low defect density, and theoretical specific surface areas for defect-free monolayers [ 44 ]. In comparison, biomass-derived graphene typically shows electrical conductivities ranging from 10 2  to 10 4  S m − 1 , specific surface areas between approximately 500 and 1800 m 2  g − 1  depending on precursor and activation process, and Raman ID/IG ratios of approximately 0.8–1.3, reflecting higher defect concentrations [ 45 ]. Although these properties are generally inferior to CVD-grown graphene, the defects and porous morphology can be advantageous for electrochemical energy storage because they provide abundant ion transport pathways and additional electrochemically active sites.

Among the available methods, CVD produces the highest-quality graphene with excellent crystallinity and electrical conductivity; however, the process requires high temperatures, costly substrates, sophisticated equipment, and additional transfer steps, resulting in elevated production costs. Mechanical exfoliation yields defect-free graphene but is unsuitable for mass production because of its low yield and labor-intensive nature. Chemical reduction of graphene oxide and liquid-phase exfoliation are considered more industrially viable due to their scalability and lower production costs, although the resulting graphene typically contains structural defects and exhibits lower conductivity than CVD-grown graphene. Emerging sustainable approaches, including biomass-derived graphene and green synthesis techniques, offer attractive pathways toward low-cost and environmentally friendly production; however, challenges related to reproducibility, quality control, and large-scale manufacturing remain unresolved. sections.heading: Properties of graphene-based Materials
paragraphs: Graphene-based materials are increasingly recognized for their extraordinary properties, which make them highly advantageous for a wide range of applications, especially in energy storage technologies. These materials are unique due to their combination of excellent structural, electrical, thermal, mechanical, and electrochemical characteristics. The lifespan, effectiveness, and performance of energy storage devices like SCs and batteries are greatly influenced by each of these characteristics. The layered architectures of rGOs were confirmed by the use of scanning and transmission electron microscopy (SEM & TEM) techniques. The structural properties of graphene-based materials, including their high surface area and porosity, make them highly effective for charge storage, enabling the development of high-capacity energy storage devices. Electrical and thermal properties are essential for ensuring that energy storage systems can charge and discharge rapidly while maintaining stability under high power and thermal conditions. Mechanical properties, including graphene’s superior strength and flexibility, open up new possibilities for developing flexible, wearable, and portable energy storage devices [ 46 ]. Lastly, electrochemical properties such as stability during charge/discharge cycles are critical for enhancing the cycling life and long-term efficiency of energy storage systems. As demonstrated in Table  2 , graphene’s strong electrical conductivity, it is the ideal material for a range of energy storage applications, including as batteries, SCs, and hybrid devices, because to its remarkable mechanical strength and thermal stability. These qualities are essential for improving energy storage systems’ durability, effectiveness, and performance. Researchers are continuously exploring ways to optimize these properties, particularly through material modifications and hybridization, in order to maximize their performance in energy storage devices. The ability to control and enhance these properties is crucial for addressing the challenges of scalability, cost, and performance in large-scale applications. Overall, the exceptional properties of graphene-based materials offer significant potential for the development of next-generation energy storage systems.

sections.heading: Structural and morphological properties
paragraphs: The structural and morphological properties of graphene-based materials are critical to their performance in energy storage applications, with several key factors contributing to their efficiencyA two-dimensional substance known for its remarkable surface area is graphene, which is composed of a single layer of hexagonally arranged carbon atoms. Graphene monolayers can have a specific surface area of about 2630 m 2 /g, offering a vast interface for charge storage. This high surface area is a significant factor in the material’s ability to store energy, directly contributing to the high capacitance observed in SCs and the high capacity in batteries.

Porosity is another important morphological feature that affects the electrochemical performance of graphene-based materials. By tailoring the size, shape, and distribution of pores, the available surface area for charge accumulation can be maximized. In SCs, this porosity is crucial for enhancing energy and power densities. Graphene-based materials with optimized pore structures have demonstrated capacitance values reaching 250 F/g and beyond, compared to conventional activated carbons, which typically offer around 100–150 F/g [ 47 ]. The presence of structural defects, such as vacancies or functional groups (e.g., hydroxyl, carboxyl), can influence the porosity and surface area, thus affecting the electrochemical performance. For example, functionalized GO can enhance the electrochemical capacitance due to the introduction of additional active sites.

The interlayer spacing in graphene-based materials also plays a significant role in their electrochemical behavior. Materials such as rGO and GO have a greater interlayer spacing compared to pristine graphene, which enables better ion diffusion in energy storage devices. GO has a large interlayer spacing (~0.8 nm), allowing for increased ion accessibility during the charge/discharge process. Studies have shown that the interlayer spacing of GO can significantly impact the energy density of SCs, with larger spacings leading to enhanced ion storage capability [ 48 ]. Furthermore, rGO has demonstrated encouraging outcomes in LIBs as an anode material, with up to 700 mAh/g of capacity gains, which is much higher than conventional graphite anodes, owing to its increased interlayer spacing and the presence of oxygen functional groups [ 49 ]. Graphene’s ability to form different nanostructures further enhances its versatility in energy storage applications. These include GO, rGO, graphene composites, and hybrid materials that can be engineered for specific applications. For example, the combination of graphene with transition metal oxides (e.g., MnO₂ or RuO₂) in hybrid systems improves electrochemical performance, offering both high conductivity and additional charge storage sites.

The synthesis method used to fabricate graphene-based materials has a significant impact on their structural and morphological properties. CVD, for instance, is known to produce high-quality graphene with fewer defects and a more ordered structure. CVD-grown graphene can achieve a sheet resistance as low as 20 Ω/sq, making it ideal for applications that require high conductivity and performance [ 50 ]. On the other hand, liquid-phase exfoliation, a more scalable method, produces graphene at a lower cost but with a higher number of defects, which can affect the material’s electrochemical behavior. Graphene produced via liquid-phase exfoliation often has a specific surface area around 800–1000 m 2 /g, which is lower than CVD-grown graphene but still suitable for many energy storage applications. Hydrothermal methods, another emerging synthesis technique, can produce GO and rGO with tunable structural properties, allowing for customization of the material for specific applications.

sections.heading: Electrical and thermal properties
paragraphs: The efficacy of graphene-based materials in energy storage devices, including batteries, SCs, and other energy conversion systems, is largely dependent on their electrical and thermal characteristics. Because of its honeycomb lattice structure, which allows π-electrons to delocalize across the carbon atoms, graphene has exceptional electrical conductivity. This delocalization allows for nearly ballistic electron transport, resulting in a low electrical resistance. The electrical conductivity of graphene can reach up to 10 6  S/m, which is over 100 times greater than copper’s conductivity (5.8 × 10 5  S/m) [ 51 ]. This makes graphene an ideal material for electrodes in energy storage applications, where fast electron flow is essential for efficient charging and discharging cycles.

The conductivity of graphene can be further enhanced by functionalization and composite formation. For instance, the incorporation of graphene into composites with metals or polymers can optimize its electrical properties for specific applications. In SCs, graphene-based materials contribute to high power densities, with some graphene-based SCs reaching power densities of over 30 kW/kg [ 52 ]. High-performance SCs require fast charge/discharge rates, which are made possible by this. Graphene can also increase the electrode materials electrical conductivity in LIBs [ 53 ], which lowers internal resistance and boosts charge/discharge efficiency. For example, the incorporation of graphene into lithium-ion battery anodes has led to improvements in cycling performance, with specific capacity values reaching 350 mAh/g, compared to around 200 mAh/g for conventional graphite. Graphene also boasts exceptional thermal conductivity, with a value of approximately 5000 W/m·K [ 54 ], far surpassing many other materials, including copper (398 W/m·K). This superior thermal conductivity enables graphene to efficiently dissipate heat generated during the charge/discharge cycles in energy storage devices. In batteries, heat generation is a critical issue, as it can lead to overheating, reduced efficiency, and, in extreme cases, thermal runaway. Graphene’s ability to conduct heat effectively helps mitigate these risks, improving the safety and stability of the device. For instance, graphene-based thermal management materials have been shown to significantly reduce the operating temperatures in LIBs, contributing to enhanced safety and longer cycle life.

In terms of thermal stability, graphene can withstand temperatures exceeding 3000 °C in an inert environment, making it highly resistant to thermal degradation [ 55 ]. This property ensures that graphene-based materials maintain their structural integrity and performance over extended periods, even in high-temperature conditions. As energy storage devices, especially batteries, generate substantial heat during cycling, the ability of graphene to maintain its structural properties at high temperatures enhances the longevity of these devices. For example, In terms of endurance and thermal stability, graphene-based SCs have proven to surpass conventional materials, exhibiting consistent performance even after 10,000 charge/discharge cycles.

sections.heading: Mechanical properties
paragraphs: Graphene-based materials exhibit exceptional mechanical properties that are critical to their performance in energy storage applications, particularly in flexible and wearable devices. These materials possess outstanding tensile strength, flexibility, and resilience, making them highly suitable for devices that demand both high performance and mechanical stability.

One of the strongest materials ever found is graphene, which has a tensile strength of up to 130 gigapascals (GPa), about 100 times more than steel’s (~1 GPa). The strong sp2 bonding between the carbon atoms in its hexagonal lattice structure is responsible for this remarkable tensile strength [ 56 ]. In energy storage applications, this strength helps ensure that the graphene-based electrodes maintain their integrity and performance over many charge/discharge cycles, thus contributing to the durability of devices such as batteries and SCs. For instance, in SCs, graphene’s strength prevents the mechanical breakdown of electrodes, which would otherwise lead to capacity degradation after repeated cycling. Moreover, graphene’s inherent flexibility is another key advantage. It is capable of bending and stretching without losing its mechanical properties, with a strain tolerance of up to 20%, far exceeding that of many other materials. This flexibility enables the integration of graphene into flexible and wearable energy storage devices, such as flexible SCs or batteries. Graphene-based energy storage devices can be bent or stretched without significant performance loss, making them ideal for applications like wearable electronics or smart textiles. This flexibility also allows these devices to conform to irregular surfaces, thus increasing their potential for use in a variety of advanced applications.

Graphene’s mechanical properties can be further tailored by combining it with other materials to create composite structures. For example, graphene/polymer composites have been shown to possess enhanced elasticity and toughness, with graphene improving the mechanical strength of the composite material by more than 50% [ 57 ]. This combination is particularly beneficial for energy storage applications where both high mechanical strength and the ability to withstand repeated deformation are essential. Additionally, graphene-based composites with metal oxides or carbon nanotubes (CNTs) can enhance the mechanical resilience and energy storage capacity of the device, allowing for more durable and efficient performance [ 58 ]. In terms of cyclic stability, graphene-based materials have demonstrated remarkable endurance. For example, in graphene-based SCs, cyclic stability of up to 10,000 charge/discharge cycles with minimal capacity loss (less than 10%) has been reported. This high level of mechanical durability ensures the longevity of the devices and enhances their viability for commercial use [ 59 ]. The ability of graphene to withstand many cycles without significant degradation or mechanical failure contributes to its appeal in energy storage applications where long-term reliability is a key factor.

sections.heading: Electrochemical properties
paragraphs: The performance of graphene-based materials in energy storage devices, especially SCs and batteries, is greatly influenced by their electrochemical characteristics. These properties, shown in Table  3  directly impact the charge/discharge cycles, energy density, power density, and cycle stability, which are key performance indicators in energy storage technologies. Electrochemical Stability Stable during multiple charge/discharge cycles Ensures a long lifespan of energy storage devices by minimizing performance degradation over time. Energy Density Up to 30 Wh/kg makes graphene-based materials perfect for energy storage applications that demand high energy output since it contributes to high energy storage capacity. Graphene’s high surface area is one of its most significant electrochemical advantages. The high surface area of graphene offering abundant sites for ion adsorption, which is vital for high capacitance in SCs and high capacity in batteries. In SCs, this leads to a large number of electrochemical active sites for ion storage, significantly enhancing the device’s energy and power densities. For instance, graphene SCs have demonstrated an energy density of up to 30–50 Wh/kg with a power density of 100 kW/kg, which is significantly higher than conventional carbon-based SCs [ 60 ]. In LIBs, graphene-based anodes exhibit substantial improvements in energy storage capacity. While graphite typically exhibits a specific capacity of ~ 350 mAh/g, graphene and GO materials can enhance this capacity. For example, graphene-based anodes in LIBs have shown capacities as high as 700 mAh/g, doubling the storage capacity of conventional graphite anodes [ 61 ]. This is attributed to graphene’s high surface area and excellent electronic conductivity, which improves the efficiency of lithium-ion insertion and extraction during cycling. Graphene-based SCs have demonstrated remarkable cycling stability, retaining over 90% of their initial capacitance after 10,000 cycles at moderate current densities, and maintaining 85% even after 15,000 cycles at higher current densities of 10 A/g. In LIBs, graphene-based anodes exhibit impressive stability, with specific capacity retention of 82% after 2000 cycles at 2 C [ 62 ], effectively mitigating issues related to volume expansion and structural degradation. Similarly, graphene-supported SIB electrodes have shown high cycling stability, maintaining 88% of their capacity after 800 cycles at 1 C, highlighting graphene’s ability to prevent electrode pulverization and maintain electrode integrity over prolonged use. Furthermore, the incorporation of dopants and surface modifications, such as nitrogen-doped graphene and graphene-MnO₂ composites, enhances graphene’s structural robustness, providing additional active sites and improving ion diffusion during cycling. These results validate graphene’s superior long-term stability across different energy storage systems, making it a prime candidate for applications requiring high cycle life.

Graphene’s excellent electrical conductivity further enhances its electrochemical performance. The intrinsic conductivity of graphene is around 10,000 S/cm, which facilitates rapid electron transport during charge and discharge cycles. This property is especially important for applications requiring high power densities, such as SCs [ 63 ]. For example, graphene SCs can achieve high charge/discharge rates, with graphene electrodes capable of discharging in less than 1 second without significant loss of energy. This is in contrast to conventional carbon-based electrodes, which may require several seconds to discharge. In LIBs, the high conductivity of graphene also minimizes internal resistance, improving the overall efficiency and allowing for faster charging times. Graphene-based anodes in LIBs have been reported to charge in less than 30 minutes compared to several hours for traditional graphite-based anodes [ 64 ]. Another crucial factor for graphene in energy storage is its electrochemical stability. Graphene-based materials exhibit impressive cycling stability due to the structural integrity of graphene. In SCs, graphene-based electrodes can withstand over 10,000 charge/discharge cycles with minimal capacitance loss. For example, graphene-based SCs can retain more than 90% of their capacitance after 10,000 cycles, whereas conventional carbon-based electrodes typically experience a greater decline in capacitance over time [ 65 ]. In batteries, graphene-based anodes show improved cycle life compared to traditional materials. A graphene-based anode for LIBs, for instance, has shown a stable capacity retention of around 85% after 1000 cycles, while a graphite anode only retains around 60–70% after the same number of cycles.

Defects and oxygen-containing functional groups present in GO and rGO play a dual role in electrochemical energy storage. Functional groups improve electrolyte wettability and provide additional active sites for ion adsorption and surface redox reactions, thereby enhancing pseudocapacitive behavior and charge-storage capability. Structural defects can also increase interlayer spacing, facilitating electrolyte penetration and ion diffusion. However, excessive oxygen functionalization disrupts the sp 2  -hybridized carbon network and reduces electrical conductivity by hindering electron transport pathways. Consequently, GO generally exhibits lower conductivity than pristine graphene, whereas rGO offers a compromise between conductivity and electrochemical activity through partial restoration of the graphitic structure. Therefore, controlling defect density and oxygen functional groups is critical for optimizing the overall electrochemical performance of graphene-based electrodes.

The functionalization of graphene also plays a significant role in its electrochemical behavior. Surface functionalization with oxygen-containing groups such as hydroxyl, carboxyl, and epoxy groups increases graphene’s hydrophilicity and ion affinity, improving its electrochemical performance, particularly in aqueous electrolytes. A study showed that GO functionalized with carboxyl groups exhibited a higher capacitance of 240 F/g compared to non-functionalized graphene, which had a capacitance of approximately 180 F/g [ 66 ]. The addition of metal oxides, like MnO₂ or RuO₂, to graphene further enhances electrochemical performance by providing additional active sites for charge storage. For instance, graphene-MnO₂ composites have been reported to exhibit a capacitance of up to 450 F/g, demonstrating a substantial improvement over pure graphene. The rate capability of graphene is another key electrochemical property [ 67 ]. The ability of graphene-based materials to maintain high performance at rapid charge/discharge rates is a major advantage. Graphene-based SCs, for example, can deliver high power densities (up to 15 kW/kg) while maintaining good energy density, making them suitable for applications requiring rapid energy release, such as electric vehicles. In LIBs, graphene-based anodes exhibit high rate capability, with graphene-oxide anode composites reaching a discharge capacity of up to 200–250 mAh/g at a high charge/discharge rate of 10 C, far surpassing the rate capabilities of traditional graphite anodes.

Doping graphene with heteroatoms such as nitrogen, sulfur, and boron alters its electronic structure, enhancing its conductivity, wettability, and electrochemical activity. For instance, nitrogen-doped graphene introduces defects that increase active sites for ion adsorption and redox reactions, thereby improving the specific capacitance of SCs and the storage capacity of LIBs. Studies have shown that nitrogen-doped graphene can achieve a specific capacitance of up to 320 F/g, compared to 240 F/g for non-doped graphene, due to increased pseudocapacitance contributions from nitrogen functional groups. Similarly, sulfur doping enhances the electrochemical performance by introducing sulfur-containing moieties that facilitate ion diffusion and improve charge storage capacity. Hybridization of graphene with other nanomaterials, such as TMOs, conductive polymers, and metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), enhances its energy storage properties by combining the high conductivity of graphene with the high capacitance and redox activity of these materials. For instance, graphene-TiO₂ hybrids exhibit improved lithium-ion diffusion and increased capacity retention, while graphene-polyaniline composites demonstrate superior pseudocapacitive behavior, offering higher capacitance and rate capability. Moreover, graphene-MnO₂ composites provide improved ion transport and additional active sites for electrochemical reactions, leading to increased energy density and cycle stability. Surface modification further enhances graphene’s interaction with electrolytes and improves ion transport efficiency.

sections.heading: Applications of graphene-based materials in energy storage
paragraphs: In SCs, graphene-based materials are particularly valued for their high surface area, which allows for significant charge storage. Increased energy and power densities are the result of these materials’ abundance of active sites. Additionally, graphene’s superior electrical conductivity facilitates rapid electron transfer during charge and discharge cycles, which further improves power density and charging speed. Because of these characteristics, graphene-based SCs are perfect for uses requiring rapid energy bursts, including electric vehicle regenerative braking systems and energy storage for renewable energy systems. Graphene’s applications extend to LIBs, where it serves in multiple roles, including as an anode, cathode, or additive. As an anode material, graphene enhances the conductivity and structural integrity of the electrode, leading to improved cycling stability and higher capacity [ 68 ]. When incorporated as a cathode material or additive, graphene helps reduce charge/discharge resistance and improves ion diffusion rates. By enhancing both capacity and cycling stability, graphene-based materials enable LIBs to overcome some of the drawbacks of traditional LIBs technologies in order to attain greater energy densities and longer lifespans. SIBs, considered an alternative to LIBs due to the abundance and low cost of sodium, encounter difficulties like poor cycling stability and a decreased energy density. Since their high surface area and conductivity can enhance the performance of both anodes and cathodes in SIBs, graphene-based materials are being investigated to address these problems. By enhancing the material’s structural stability and ion diffusion properties, graphene helps mitigate some of the challenges faced by SIBs, offering a more efficient and cost-effective energy storage solution [ 69 ]. Hybrid graphene-based materials, which combine graphene with metal oxides, polymers, or other nanomaterials, have gained significant attention due to their synergistic effects. The addition of metal oxides or polymers enhances the overall electrochemical performance, leading to improved energy storage capabilities. These hybrid materials leverage the unique properties of each component, such as the high conductivity of graphene and the high capacitance or stability of metal oxides, resulting in materials that outperform traditional materials in both energy and power densities. Emerging applications of graphene-based materials are also gaining momentum, particularly in the fields of wearable devices, flexible electronics, and solid-state batteries. Graphene’s flexibility, mechanical strength, and conductivity make it an ideal candidate for next-generation wearable devices and flexible electronics [ 70 ], where lightweight and durable materials are essential. In solid-state batteries, graphene-based materials are being explored for their ability to enhance conductivity and stability, which are crucial for improving the performance and safety of these next-generation batteries. Table  2  shows, graphene-based materials performance characteristics across different energy storage applications.

Graphene-based materials are playing a crucial role in revolutionizing energy storage technologies. By enhancing the performance of SCs, lithium-ion and SIBs, and emerging hybrid systems, graphene offers promising solutions to some of the key challenges in energy storage. With continuous advancements in synthesis methods and material composites, the future of graphene-based energy storage devices looks increasingly promising.

sections.heading: Graphene in supercapacitors
paragraphs: Graphene-based materials have demonstrated remarkable improvements in the performance of SCs, particularly in enhancing both energy and power densities. One of the key factors contributing to these improvements is the extremely high surface area of graphene. This large surface area provides a greater number of active sites for charge storage, leading to increased energy density.

Graphene’s exceptional electrical conductivity, which can reach up to 10 6  S/m, is another critical factor that enhances the performance of SCs [ 71 ]. This high conductivity allows for rapid electron movement, enabling quick charge and discharge cycles. As a result, graphene-based SCs can achieve power densities up to 100 kW/kg, making them ideal for applications requiring high-power delivery. In comparison, traditional SCs based on activated carbon typically offer power densities in the range of 10–20 kW/kg [ 72 ]. The integration of graphene with other materials, such as metal oxides and conductive polymers, has further advanced the performance of SCs. For instance, hybrid SCs that combine graphene with manganese oxide or nickel oxide have demonstrated energy densities exceeding 40 Wh/kg and power densities up to 120 kW/kg [ 73 ]. The drawbacks of conventional SCs are addressed by this combination, which takes advantage of graphene’s high conductivity and metal oxides’ high capacitance to create systems with high energy and power densities. In addition to energy and power densities, graphene’s structural stability contributes to long cycle life. Studies have shown that graphene-based SCs can endure more than 1 million charge/discharge cycles with minimal degradation, while conventional SCs typically endure around 100,000 cycles [ 74 ]. This longevity is crucial for applications in electric vehicles, renewable energy storage, and other high-performance energy storage systems.

Carbonization, graphitization, and activation methods are used to create hierarchically porous graphene-based carbons (BGCs) from a biomass carbon source, as seen in Fig.  2 . With a high specific capacitance of 175 F/g and a specific surface area (SSA) of 3,657 m 2 /g, these BGCs showed exceptional rate capabilities in an ionic liquid electrolyte. In order to maximize ion transport and electric double-layer creation, the activation process added a significant number of micro- and mesopores to the 3D macroporous carbon structure. With a maximum energy density of 74 Wh/kg and a power density of 408 kW/kg, the SCs made of these materials were competitive with the most advanced carbon electrodes. These findings demonstrate how well micro- and mesopores can be incorporated into macroporous scaffolds to improve electrochemical performance The well-developed porous network not only increases ion-accessible surface area but also facilitates rapid electrolyte penetration, leading to improved electrochemical kinetics and superior rate capabilities. Moreover, the high surface area and excellent electrical conductivity of BGCs contribute to their remarkable energy and power densities, making them suitable for high-performance supercapacitor applications. sections.heading: Graphene in lithium-ion batteries (LIBs)
paragraphs: Because of their high surface area, mechanical strength, and better electrical conductivity, graphene-based materials have demonstrated great potential in LIBs. Graphene can be used as an anode, cathode, or additive to improve electrochemical performance, such as capacity, cycling stability, and overall battery efficiency.

As an anode material, graphene-based composites have shown substantial improvements in both capacity and cycling stability compared to conventional graphite anodes. For example, a composite of GO and silicon nanoparticles demonstrated an initial discharge capacity of 1626 mAh/g at a current density of 100 mA/g, which is significantly higher than the theoretical capacity of graphite, which is 372 mAh/g. Additionally, after 500 cycles, the composite retained 80% of its initial capacity, showcasing excellent cycling stability. The high conductivity of graphene further contributes to efficient electron transport, which enhances charge/discharge processes, especially at high current densities. To enhance electrochemical performance, graphene composites are also utilized in cathodes. For instance, a graphene and LiFePO₄ combination showed a specific capacity of 160 mAh/g at a rate of 0.1 C, but pure LiFePO₄ only demonstrated 140 mAh/g [ 76 ]. Faster cycles of charge and discharge were made possible by the addition of graphene, which improved the electrochemical conductivity and rate capability. Additionally, the graphene-LiFePO₄ composite’s cycling stability was enhanced, retaining 93% of its initial capacity after 1000 cycles. The improvement is attributed to graphene’s ability to enhance electron conductivity and prevent the agglomeration of cathode particles, improving long-term stability. Graphene’s role as an additive has also proven beneficial in enhancing the performance of both anode and cathode materials in LIBs. In a study on LiCoO₂ cathodes, the addition of graphene led to a specific capacity of 185 mAh/g at a 0.5 C rate, compared to 155 mAh/g for pure LiCoO₂. This improvement in performance is due to graphene’s ability to increase electron transport pathways and offer additional active locations for the storage of lithium ions. With an initial capacity of 1485 mAh/g at 100 mA/g and 75% capacity retention after 500 cycles, GO’s addition to silicon anodes also shown a notable boost in capacity and cycling stability, compared to a loss of over 50% capacity in pure silicon anodes.

Graphene-based materials have demonstrated improvements in both capacity and cycling stability. For example, a graphene-coated SiO₂ composite achieved a capacity of 1720 mAh/g at a current density of 0.1 A/g, which is significantly higher than conventional graphite anodes. This composite retained 92% of its initial capacity after 300 cycles, compared to less than 60% retention in pure SiO₂ anodes. The graphene coating helps buffer the volume expansion of silicon during lithiation and delithiation, preventing material degradation and improving the structural stability of the anode. Additionally, graphene’s high conductivity improves electron flow, reducing internal resistance and enhancing energy density and power density. In cathodes, graphene composites also show notable improvements. A composite of LiNi 0.6 Co 0.3 Mn 0.4 O 2  modified with GO demonstrated a specific capacity of 195 mAh/g at a 1 C rate, retaining 87% capacity after 1000 cycles. These results highlight graphene’s contribution to both rate capability and cycle life, preventing particle aggregation and enhancing conductivity.

Figure  3  provide comprehensive insights into the superior performance of Si/graphene composites as anode materials. The cycling stability of Si/graphene composites was tested under various Si-to-graphene weight ratios, revealing that the composite structure significantly enhances cycle life. The best-performing composite, with a 65% Si nanoparticle and 35% graphene ratio, exhibited a capacity retention of over 85% after 100 cycles at a current density of 100 mA/g, demonstrating its long-term stability [ 78 ]. The rate performance studies showed that the Si/graphene composite maintained a high reversible capacity even at high current densities, indicating excellent power capability. The charge/discharge profiles recorded after 1, 2, 4, 50, 80, and 100 cycles demonstrated a gradual and stable voltage profile, with minimal fading, confirming the composite’s structural integrity over prolonged cycling. The presence of graphene prevented volume expansion and pulverization of Si nanoparticles, which is a common issue in Si-based anodes. The CV curves of the 65% Si nanoparticles/35% graphene composite, measured at a scan rate of 0.1 mV/s, showed distinct redox peaks corresponding to the lithiation and delithiation of silicon, further validating the composite’s high electrochemical activity. The material exhibited a high initial Coulombic efficiency, indicating effective lithium-ion storage and transport. Moreover, the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy results indicated that the Si/graphene composite had a lower charge transfer resistance compared to pure silicon, suggesting improved electron conductivity and lithium-ion diffusion. The Nyquist plots confirmed that the composite maintained a stable interfacial resistance over cycling, preventing capacity degradation. With their high capacity, outstanding cycling stability, superior rate capability, and low charge transfer resistance, Si nanoparticles embedded in graphene sheets are a great high-performance anode material for LIBs, according to these electrochemical studies. This makes them ideal for next-generation energy storage applications.
