These improvements make graphene-based materials a promising solution for enhancing LIB performance, providing more efficient and long-lasting energy storage devices for a wide range of applications, including electric vehicles and portable electronics.

sections.heading: Graphene in sodium-ion batteries (SIBs)
paragraphs: SIBs have gained attention as a cost-effective and sustainable alternative due to the natural abundance of sodium. However, challenges such as the larger ionic radius of Na +  (1.02 Å vs. 0.76 Å for Li + ), slower ion diffusion kinetics, structural instability, and limited electrode materials hinder their practical applications. Because of its remarkable electrical conductivity, large surface area, mechanical flexibility, and capacity to support volume expansion during charge-discharge cycles, graphene has become a viable material to address these issues.

Graphene and its derivatives, including rGO and graphene composites, have demonstrated excellent sodium storage performance. Experimental results have indicated capacities in the range of 200 to 300 mAh g − 1  with long cycle life, although theoretical studies suggest a sodium storage capacity of approximately 335 mAh g − 1  for graphene. Oxygen-containing functional groups are reported to enhance Na +  storage by improving surface wettability and providing additional active adsorption sites, as supported by XPS and DFT studies reported in the literature [ 79 ,  80 ]. GO’s oxygen-containing functional groups make Na +  intercalation easier, while rGO enhances electronic conductivity, leading to improved electrochemical performance. Graphene-based composite anodes further enhance Na +  storage properties. For example, SnO₂/graphene composites exhibit reversible capacities exceeding 400 mAh g − 1  at a current density of 0.1 A g − 1 , with stable performance over 200 cycles. Similarly, Fe₂O₃/graphene anodes demonstrate capacities of ~ 300 mAh g − 1  with minimal capacity fading over 500 cycles, attributed to graphene’s role in buffering volume expansion and maintaining structural integrity.

Sodium-ion cathode materials, such as layered oxides (NaₓCoO₂, NaₓMnO₂) and polyanionic compounds (Na₃V₂(PO₄)₃, NaFePO₄), often suffer from poor electronic conductivity and structural degradation. Incorporating graphene into these materials significantly improves charge transfer kinetics and electrode stability. Na₃V₂(PO₄)₃/graphene composites have demonstrated high capacities (~110 mAh g − 1  at 1C) with excellent rate performance, while NaFePO₄ coated with graphene exhibits enhanced cycling stability and higher sodium diffusion rates. Graphene-based electrodes enable fast charge/discharge rates in SIBs due to their superior electrical conductivity. rGO anodes retain a capacity of ~ 180 mAh g − 1  even at high current densities (5 A g − 1 ), highlighting their excellent rate performance. Additionally, graphene-based electrodes exhibit long-term cycling stability, with minimal capacity degradation (~1% over 1000 cycles), making them promising candidates for large-scale energy storage applications.

Na₃V₂(PO₄)₃/C (NVP/C) and its graphene-enhanced counterpart, Na₃V₂(PO₄)₃/C-G (NVP/C-G), are promising cathode materials for SIBs, as demonstrated in the Fig.  4 . The incorporation of rGO into NVP/C significantly enhances its electrochemical performance by improving bulk phase conductivity and reducing polarization. The SEM images (Fig.  4 (a)) confirm the uniform dispersion of NVP/C and NVP/C-G composites, ensuring efficient electron and ion transport pathways. The Figure  4 (b) reveal that NVP/C-G maintains 92.3% and 92.1% of its initial capacity after 500 cycles at 0.5 C and 2 C, respectively, which is markedly superior to NVP/C suggest that these materials can withstand prolonged charge/discharge cycles, which is essential for reliable grid-scale energy storage. The charge/discharge profiles at 0.1 C (Fig.  4 (c)) demonstrate that NVP/C-G delivers a higher discharge capacity of 103.5 mAh g − 1 , indicating improved sodium-ion storage capability. Moreover, the rate performance tests highlight that NVP/C-G outperforms NVP/C, showcasing its ability to sustain capacity at varying charge/discharge rates. Nyquist plots (Fig.  4 (c)) confirm lower charge-transfer resistance for NVP/C-G, which translates to enhanced ionic and electronic conductivity. The cycling performance at 2 C (Fig.  4 (d)) further emphasizes the long-term stability of NVP/C-G, as its charge/discharge profiles remain stable over multiple cycles. The improved electrochemical properties of NVP/C-G are attributed to the synergistic effect of graphene, which acts as a conductive network, decreasing polarization and enhancing sodium-ion diffusion. Furthermore, the enhanced rate capability, as demonstrated by the sustained capacity at different C-rates (Fig.  4 (c)), underscores the suitability of NVP/C-G composites for high-power applications. These results establish NVP/C-G as a highly efficient cathode material for SIBs, providing high capacity, excellent rate capability, and outstanding cycling stability. sections.heading: Hybrid graphene-based materials
paragraphs: Hybrid graphene-based materials have gained significant attention due to their ability to enhance electrochemical, mechanical, and structural properties for various energy storage and conversion applications. By incorporating metal oxides, polymers, or other nanomaterials, graphene-based composites exhibit improved conductivity, structural stability, and energy storage capabilities, making them suitable for high-performance batteries, SCs, and fuel cells.

Graphene combined with metal oxides (GMOs) forms a highly efficient hybrid material, particularly for energy storage applications such as LIBs and SCsAlthough metal oxides with high theoretical capacities, such as TiO₂, MnO₂, FeO₃, CoO₄, and SnO₂, have low electrical conductivity and experience significant volume expansion during charge/discharge cycles. Graphene acts as a conductive support, mitigating these drawbacks and improving rate performance and cycling stability. For instance, graphene-TiO₂ composites exhibit enhanced lithium-ion diffusion kinetics and improved cycling stability due to the synergy between TiO₂ nanoparticles and graphene sheets. Electrochemical studies show that TiO₂/graphene composites deliver a stable capacity of over 200 mAh g − 1  at 10 C, much higher than pure TiO₂ (80 mAh g − 1 ). Similarly, MnO₂/graphene composites, widely used in SCs, achieve a high specific capacitance of over 350 F g − 1  due to their large electrochemical surface area and fast charge transport pathways.

Graphene-polymer hybrids are extensively utilized in flexible energy storage devices due to their lightweight nature, mechanical flexibility, and tunable electronic properties. Conducting polymers such as polyaniline (PANI), polypyrrole (PPy), and poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) (PEDOT) are commonly used with graphene to enhance charge storage and mechanical strength. For example, graphene-PANI composites exhibit superior electrochemical performance in SCs, delivering a specific capacitance of ~ 750 F g − 1  with high stability over 10,000 cycles. The π-π interactions between graphene and polymer chains facilitate rapid electron transport, improving rate performance. Additionally, polymer-wrapped graphene composites prevent aggregation of graphene sheets, maintaining a high electrochemical surface area and improving mechanical flexibility for wearable electronics.

Graphene hybridized with other nanomaterials, such as CNTs, MXenes, and transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), enhances energy storage and electrocatalytic properties. Graphene-CNT Composites: The combination of graphene and CNTs creates a 3D conductive framework with high surface area, improving ion diffusion and charge transport in batteries and SCs. Studies have shown that graphene-CNT hybrids achieve ultrahigh capacitance (~1200 F g − 1 ) and excellent rate capability. Graphene-MXene Composites: MXenes (Ti₃C₂Tₓ, V₂C, etc.) are emerging 2D materials with metallic conductivity and hydrophilic nature. When combined with graphene, MXene-graphene composites exhibit enhanced lithium/sodium storage capacity, with Ti₃C₂Tₓ/graphene electrodes delivering > 400 mAh g − 1  at 2 C in LIBs [ 64 ]. Graphene-TMD Composites: Transition metal dichalcogenides (MoS₂, WS₂) provide high theoretical capacities for energy storage. MoS₂/graphene composites, for example, demonstrate excellent sodium storage performance with capacities exceeding 500 mAh g − 1  at 1 C. The flexible graphene network prevents TMD layer restacking, maintaining high electrochemical activity over extended cycling.

Hybrid graphene-based materials have found extensive applications across diverse energy storage systems due to their synergistic properties. In supercapacitors, graphene combined with metal oxides (e.g., MnO₂, RuO₂) or conducting polymers (e.g., polyaniline, polypyrrole) enhances capacitance and charge transfer by improving electrical conductivity and active surface area. In lithium-ion and sodium-ion batteries, graphene–metal oxide hybrids facilitate faster ion diffusion and structural stability during cycling, resulting in higher energy density and longer lifespan. Similarly, graphene–carbon nanotube composites provide robust 3D conductive frameworks that prevent restacking and improve electrolyte accessibility. These hybrid architectures bridge the gap between high power and high energy performance, making them promising candidates for next-generation energy storage technologies.

Their synergistic properties improve electrical conductivity, mechanical strength, ion diffusion, and cycling stability, making them suitable for LIBs/SIBs, SCs, and flexible electronics. Future research will focus on scalable synthesis methods and optimizing material structures for commercial implementation.

sections.heading: Emerging applications
paragraphs: Graphene-based materials have shown tremendous potential in emerging applications such as wearable devices, flexible electronics, and solid-state batteries, largely due to their unique properties, including high electrical conductivity, mechanical strength, flexibility, and large surface area. In wearable devices, graphene’s superior conductivity and mechanical performance make it an ideal candidate for flexible sensors, electronic skins, and energy-harvesting systems. Recent studies have shown that graphene-based sensors exhibit a significant conductivity enhancement, up to 1000%, compared to traditional materials like silver inks. Additionally, graphene’s tensile strength (over 130 GPa) and flexibility (enduring over 10,000 bending cycles) allow it to maintain performance in e-skin sensors that require both stretchability and durability. Graphene-based triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) have also been demonstrated to achieve power densities of up to 50 mW/m 2 , making them suitable for self-powered wearable devices and health-monitoring applications.

In flexible electronics, graphene’s combination of transparency (90%) and low sheet resistance (as low as 100 Ω/sq) enables its use in transparent conductive films for flexible touchscreens and displays. For instance, graphene electrodes in organic light-emitting diode (OLED) displays have improved efficiency by 30% and reduced power consumption by 15% compared to conventional indium tin oxide (ITO) electrodes. Furthermore, graphene-based stretchable circuits can endure strains of up to 100% without significant electrical performance loss, making them ideal for next-generation flexible electronics. A recent study demonstrated that graphene-based conductors maintained 95% of their conductivity even after being stretched to twice their original length.

Additionally, graphene is essential to the development of solid-state batteries (SSBs), providing enhancements in stability and energy density. Graphene composites have been explored as anode and cathode materials in solid-state lithium batteries, showing up to a 50% increase in specific capacity compared to traditional graphite anodes. Moreover, graphene-enhanced solid-state electrolytes have achieved ionic conductivities of 10 − 3  S/cm, comparable to that of liquid electrolytes, while also improving the stability of the solid electrolyte interface (SEI), reducing capacity degradation. Graphene-enhanced solid-state batteries are a promising option for use in electric vehicles and large-scale energy storage systems because solid-state lithium batteries employing graphene-based materials have shown energy densities of up to 550 Wh/kg, which is 25% higher than traditional LIBs.

A major limitation is the restacking of graphene sheets caused by strong π–π interactions, which decreases the accessible surface area and reduces ion transport efficiency. Maintaining strong interfacial adhesion between graphene electrodes and flexible substrates is another critical challenge, as delamination can occur under cyclic mechanical stress. Environmental factors such as humidity, temperature fluctuations, and exposure to sweat may further affect device stability and durability. Moreover, the large-scale production of defect-controlled graphene with consistent quality remains costly and technically challenging.

sections.heading: Sustainability, economic viability, and policy implications
paragraphs: The integration of graphene-based materials into energy storage applications must be evaluated not only for their performance but also for their sustainability and economic feasibility. Sustainable synthesis methods play a crucial role in ensuring that graphene production aligns with environmental goals. Biomass-derived graphene, produced from renewable resources such as plant-based materials or waste products, is gaining attention as a greener alternative to conventional synthesis methods. By leveraging green chemistry approaches, such as the reduction of GO using environmentally benign reducing agents, the environmental impact of graphene production can be minimized, contributing to the broader goals of sustainability. Additionally, the use of water-based solvents and lower temperature processes can further reduce the energy consumption associated with graphene synthesis. Economic feasibility is another critical consideration in the commercialization of graphene-based energy storage technologies. While graphene exhibits exceptional properties, the high cost of production remains a significant barrier to large-scale adoption [ 83 ]. Cost-effective production techniques, such as the development of scalable CVD methods, and optimization of biomass-derived graphene processes, can help reduce overall production costs. Moreover, recycling of graphene from used devices or waste materials may further lower costs and improve the material’s overall economic viability. Collaborative efforts between industries and research institutions are vital for developing these cost-reduction strategies and ensuring the economic sustainability of graphene technologies. The sustainability of graphene-based energy storage technologies depends on addressing both production costs and environmental concerns. While graphene offers exceptional electrochemical properties, high production costs remain a significant barrier to commercialization. To overcome this, optimizing scalable techniques such as plasma-enhanced CVD and direct graphite exfoliation can help reduce manufacturing expenses without compromising quality. Additionally, environmental concerns associated with conventional graphene production, such as high energy consumption and hazardous by-products, can be mitigated by adopting greener synthesis methods like biomass-derived graphene and electrochemical exfoliation. Life cycle analysis (LCA) studies highlight that these approaches minimize environmental impact, making graphene production more sustainable. Furthermore, developing efficient recycling protocols for graphene-based devices can reduce electronic waste and support a circular economy. Collaborative efforts between industries, research institutions, and policymakers are essential to establishing cost-effective production methods, ensuring environmental responsibility, and promoting the large-scale adoption of graphene-based energy storage technologies.

The commercialization of graphene-based energy storage technologies and their market viability, it is essential to highlight recent progress made by industry leaders and emerging startups. Companies such as Skeleton Technologies and Nanotech Energy have successfully developed graphene-based supercapacitors with high energy densities, superior power output, and long cycle life, making them attractive for applications in electric vehicles, grid stabilization, and consumer electronics. Skeleton Technologies ultracapacitors, for instance, demonstrate energy densities of up to 20 Wh/kg, significantly outperforming traditional activated carbon-based capacitors. Similarly, Nanotech Energy has pioneered graphene-enhanced batteries that offer improved thermal stability and fast-charging capabilities. Moreover, the commercialization of graphene-based LIBs has gained momentum, with several companies incorporating graphene as an anode material to enhance ion transport and cycling stability. Log9 Materials has developed graphene-based aluminum fuel cells with extended operational lifespans and higher efficiency, while Real Graphene focuses on graphene-enhanced LIBs that promise faster charging and enhanced safety. Despite these advancements, widespread market penetration remains limited due to the high cost of graphene production and challenges in scaling up manufacturing processes. Addressing these challenges requires continued advancements in cost-effective production methods, such as improved CVD processes and more efficient reduction of GO using green and scalable techniques. Additionally, integrating graphene with existing battery technologies must be optimized to balance performance improvements with cost-efficiency. As the global energy storage market continues to grow, the development of standardized manufacturing protocols and quality control measures will play a pivotal role in ensuring the large-scale adoption of graphene-based technologies, thereby enhancing their commercial viability.

Policy and governmental support play an essential role in accelerating the commercialization of graphene technologies. Governments can provide incentives, such as subsidies and grants, to support research and development (R&D) of graphene-based materials, making it more attractive for industries to invest in these technologies [ 84 ]. Additionally, fostering public-private partnerships can facilitate the transition from lab-scale prototypes to commercial products. Scaling up research from laboratory settings to real-world applications requires not only technological advancements but also a supportive regulatory environment that promotes innovation and market entry. Policymakers must also address safety standards and environmental regulations to ensure the responsible use of graphene in energy storage systems, thereby ensuring long-term commercial success. International collaboration could also be key to overcoming the challenges of scaling graphene-based technologies, as shared knowledge and resources could drive faster advancements. For graphene-based energy storage technologies to become economically viable and sustainable, advancements in green synthesis methods, cost-reduction strategies, and supportive policy frameworks are crucial. With the right incentives and scaling strategies, graphene can play a transformative role in the future of energy storage. To accelerate the commercialization of graphene-based energy storage technologies, several targeted policy instruments can be highly effective. These include R&D subsidies and innovation grants to support early-stage material development, and tax credits or production-linked incentives to encourage industrial-scale manufacturing. Additionally, public procurement programs can create early market demand by integrating graphene-based devices into grid storage and transportation applications. Support for pilot-scale demonstration projects can bridge the gap between laboratory research and commercial deployment. Furthermore, establishing standardization and certification frameworks for graphene materials will ensure quality consistency and improve investor confidence. Finally, incentives for green manufacturing practices, such as reduced taxes for low-emission synthesis routes, can align commercialization with sustainability goals.

Despite promising laboratory outcomes, the large-scale commercialization of graphene-based energy storage devices faces several bottlenecks. High production costs, inconsistent material quality, and the absence of standardized manufacturing protocols hinder market translation. Establishing scalable synthesis routes that ensure uniformity and reproducibility is essential for industrial adoption. Furthermore, the lack of clear policy frameworks, safety regulations, and standardized testing procedures creates uncertainty for investors and manufacturers. Addressing these challenges requires integrated efforts across academia, industry, and government to develop cost-effective manufacturing infrastructure, implement certification standards, and introduce policy incentives that support sustainable commercialization of graphene technologies.

These case studies highlight the advances in graphene’s role in SCs, LIBs, SIBs, and hybrid materials for solid-state energy storage devices. By reviewing recent studies and experimental results, we can better understand how graphene is contributing to the development of next-generation energy storage technologies. The exceptional energy and power densities of GO-based SCs have prompted extensive research. These SCs leverage the unique properties of GO to offer high capacitance, cycling stability, and fast charge/discharge rates, making them an attractive option for applications in portable electronics, electric vehicles, and hybrid systems. Various research studies have demonstrated the enhancement of specific capacitances, such as those achieved by GO composites, which outpace traditional carbon-based SCs. Graphene’s role in LIBs and SIBs has been transformative, especially in improving anode and cathode materials. Graphene composites are increasingly being used in LIBs to enhance the capacity, stability, and fast charging capabilities of these batteries. In SIBs, graphene materials help address challenges related to the larger ionic radius of sodium compared to lithium, thereby improving performance. Case studies show improvements in specific capacity, cycle life, and overall energy density when graphene is incorporated into these systems. The use of graphene in solid-state systems, particularly for flexible and wearable energy storage devices, has garnered significant interest [ 84 ]. Hybrid graphene materials, such as GO combined with metal oxides or ceramics, have been used in solid-state batteries, contributing to improved safety, energy density, and mechanical flexibility. Case studies in flexible electronics and wearable devices demonstrate the potential of graphene-based solid-state energy storage devices, where their ability to retain performance even under mechanical stress is critical.

sections.heading: Supercapacitors using graphene oxide
paragraphs: GO-based SCs have demonstrated remarkable electrochemical performance, making them highly suitable for next-generation energy storage applications. Increased charge storage and better ion transport are made possible by GO’s special qualities, which include its huge surface area, adjustable oxygen functional groups, and superior dispersibility. Several real-world studies have shown that GO-based s achieve high energy density, fast charge-discharge rates, and long-term stability.

One study focused on the development of a flexible SC using rGO and PANI as active electrode materials. The rGO-PANI hybrid structure exhibited an impressive specific capacitance of 800 F g − 1  at 1 A g − 1 , significantly outperforming pristine GO-based electrodes. The SC retained 92% of its capacitance after 5000 charge-discharge cycles, highlighting its excellent durability. Additionally, the flexibility of the electrode material made it highly suitable for wearable electronics and energy storage textiles, demonstrating its potential for real-world applications. Another research study explored the electrochemical performance of (GO/CNT hybrid electrodes in aqueous SCs. The hybrid material achieved a specific energy density of 40 Wh kg − 1 , which is comparable to commercial SCs, while maintaining a high power density exceeding 15 kW kg − 1  [ 86 ]. The device exhibited outstanding cycling stability, maintaining performance over more than 20,000 charge-discharge cycles with minimal degradation. The study confirmed that the synergistic combination of GO and CNTs enhances electrical conductivity and electrolyte accessibility, leading to improved energy storage capabilities [ 87 ]. In industrial-scale applications, a company specializing in energy storage technologies developed a GO-based SC module for smart grid systems. The SC demonstrated rapid charge capability, reaching full charge within seconds while minimizing energy losses. The system was designed for long-term operation, with a lifespan exceeding one million cycles, making it a viable alternative to traditional batteries for grid stabilization. The company also emphasized the environmental benefits of GO-based electrodes, as they were synthesized using a sustainable and scalable production method.

These case studies illustrate the significant advantages of GO-based SCs in both research and industrial applications. Their high capacitance, rapid charge-discharge ability, and long cycle life make them ideal candidates for a wide range of energy storage needs, from portable electronics to large-scale energy grids. Further research is expected to refine electrode architectures and electrolyte compositions to push the performance of these SCs even further.

sections.heading: Graphene-based LIBs and SIBs [ 88 ]
paragraphs: Graphene-based LIBs and SIBs have shown remarkable improvements in electrochemical performance due to graphene’s high electrical conductivity, large surface area, and mechanical stability. Several research studies have demonstrated how incorporating graphene enhances energy storage efficiency, rate capability, and cycle life in both LIBs and SIBs.

One study focused on graphene-silicon (Si) composite anodes for LIBs, addressing the challenge of Si’s volume expansion during lithiation. The study reported that a Si/graphene composite anode with a graphene content of 35% delivered an initial specific capacity of 2650 mAh g − 1  at 0.1 C, significantly higher than conventional graphite anodes. Additionally, the composite retained 85% of its capacity after 200 charge-discharge cycles at 1 C [ 89 ], demonstrating improved cycling stability due to the flexible graphene matrix, which accommodated Si expansion and prevented electrode degradation. Another research study investigated the use of graphene-wrapped LiFePO₄ (LFP) cathodes in LIBs to enhance electronic conductivity and ion transport. The graphene-coated LFP electrodes exhibited a discharge capacity of 165 mAh g − 1  at 0.1 C [ 88 ], maintaining 92% capacity retention over 1000 cycles. Compared to standard LFP electrodes, the graphene-based cathodes demonstrated a 40% improvement in rate capability, highlighting their potential for high-power applications. For SIBs, a recent study explored the performance of graphene-supported Na₃V₂(PO₄)₃/C (NVP/C) cathodes. The introduction of graphene into the NVP/C matrix reduced internal resistance and improved charge transfer kinetics, resulting in an enhanced discharge capacity of 103.5 mAh g − 1  at 0.1 C [ 90 ]. After 500 cycles at 2 C, the NVP/C-graphene composite retained 92.1% of its capacity, significantly outperforming non-graphene NVP/C electrodes. The study confirmed that the graphene framework facilitated fast sodium-ion diffusion and maintained electrode integrity over prolonged cycling. A separate study investigated graphene-based hard carbon anodes for SIBs, addressing the challenge of low initial Coulombic efficiency (ICE) in traditional hard carbon materials. The graphene-modified anode exhibited an ICE of 85%, compared to 65% for conventional hard carbon [ 91 ]. The improved ICE, along with a stable cycling performance of 300 mAh g − 1  after 500 cycles at 1 C, demonstrated graphene’s role in enhancing sodium-ion storage kinetics and reducing irreversible capacity loss. The cracked cowpea-like structure improves ion diffusion and electron transport, resulting in high specific capacity and superior cycling stability. The study demonstrates the material’s potential as a promising anode for next-generation LIBs [ 92 ].

Graphene’s effectiveness varies significantly across LIBs, SIBs, and SCs due to differences in their underlying charge storage mechanisms. In LIBs, graphene primarily enhances anode and cathode materials by improving electronic conductivity and accommodating volume changes during lithiation, resulting in higher energy density (150–250 Wh/kg) and extended cycle life [ 93 ,  94 ]. SIBs, while offering similar benefits, exhibit lower energy density (~100–150 Wh/kg) due to the larger ionic radius of Na + , which slows down ion diffusion. However, graphene mitigates these limitations by providing faster ion transport pathways, maintaining structural stability, and improving cycle life. In contrast, SCs leverage graphene’s high surface area and electrical conductivity to achieve rapid charge-discharge rates, high power densities (up to 15 kW/kg), and excellent cycling stability (>1 million cycles). However, the energy density of SCs (~30–50 Wh/kg) remains lower compared to LIBs and SIBs, limiting their use in applications requiring long-term energy storage. While graphene significantly improves performance across all three technologies, its effectiveness is most pronounced in SCs, where it optimizes high-rate capabilities and cycle stability, making it ideal for applications requiring instantaneous power delivery.

sections.heading: Hybrid graphene materials in solid-state systems
paragraphs: For next-generation solid-state energy storage devices, hybrid graphene-based materials have been thoroughly researched, especially for flexible and wearable electronics. The combination of graphene with polymers, metal oxides, and other nanomaterials has led to the development of solid-state LIBs and SIBs, as well as SCs with enhanced electrochemical performance, mechanical flexibility, and safety.

One significant study investigated a graphene-based solid-state lithium-ion battery (SSLIB) incorporating a hybrid polymer electrolyte. The battery utilized a composite electrolyte consisting of polyethylene oxide (PEO) and graphene nanosheets, which improved ionic conductivity while maintaining mechanical flexibility. The SSLIB demonstrated a remarkable 92% capacity retention after 500 cycles at ambient temperature, and a high specific capacity of 160 mAh g − 1  at 0.2 C [ 95 ]. Compared to conventional liquid electrolyte-based LIBs, this solid-state system exhibited improved thermal stability and minimized the risk of electrolyte leakage, making it an ideal candidate for wearable applications. Another research study explored a graphene-wrapped Na₃V₂(PO₄)₃ (NVP) cathode integrated with a solid-state sodium-ion battery (SSIB). The hybrid material enhanced Na-ion transport and electronic conductivity, enabling a discharge capacity of 120 mAh g − 1  at 0.1 C with outstanding rate capability. Even after 1000 cycles at 5 C [ 96 ], the graphene-based solid-state SIB retained over 90% of its capacity, significantly outperforming conventional SIBs. The flexible nature of the solid electrolyte allowed seamless integration into bendable energy storage systems, demonstrating potential for self-powered wearable electronics. In the field of flexible SCs, hybrid graphene aerogels doped with metal oxides such as MnO₂ and RuO₂ have shown outstanding performance in solid-state configurations [ 97 ]. A recent study reported that a flexible graphene/MnO₂ aerogel SC delivered an areal capacitance of 500 mF cm − 2 , with excellent mechanical stability under repeated bending cycles. Additionally, following 10,000 cycles, a graphene-polymer composite solid-state SC retained 95% of its capacitance and demonstrated an energy density of 12 Wh kg − 1  [ 98 ]. These developments validate that graphene’s excellent conductivity and surface area, when combined with appropriate nanomaterials, can significantly enhance charge storage and mechanical durability in flexible energy devices. Additionally, graphene has been integrated into flexible all-solid-state micro-SCs (ASMSCs), which are critical for miniaturized electronics. A study on graphene/CNT hybrid ASMSCs demonstrated exceptional volumetric capacitance of 150 F cm − 3 , surpassing conventional planar micro-SCs. These devices retained 98% of their capacitance after 50,000 cycles, highlighting their long-term reliability for next-generation smart textiles and biomedical implants.

Graphene-based materials demonstrate superior electrochemical performance compared to conventional electrode materials such as CNTs and TMOs due to their high electrical conductivity, large surface area, and mechanical flexibility. A comparative study of SCs revealed that graphene-based electrodes achieved a specific capacitance of 800 F/g at 1 A/g, significantly surpassing CNT-based electrodes, which typically exhibit capacitances in the range of 150–300 F/g. In LIBs, graphene-silicon composites exhibited an initial specific capacity of 2650 mAh/g at 0.1 C, whereas CNT-based anodes demonstrated a maximum capacity of 1200 mAh/g [ 99 ]. Similarly, graphene-coated LiFePO₄ cathodes in LIBs delivered a discharge capacity of 165 mAh/g with 92% retention over 1000 cycles, outperforming TMO-based cathodes, which often suffer from lower rate capabilities and cycling stability. Furthermore, in SIBs, graphene-supported Na₃V₂(PO₄)₃/C (NVP/C) composites demonstrated enhanced capacity retention of 92.1% after 500 cycles, whereas TMO-based electrodes typically show higher capacity fading over prolonged cycling. These quantitative comparisons highlight that graphene-based materials consistently outperform CNTs and TMOs, making them promising candidates for next-generation energy storage technologies.

sections.heading: Challenges and future directions
paragraphs: The scalable and cost-effective synthesis of graphene remains one of the most critical challenges limiting its widespread industrial adoption. Although laboratory-scale techniques such as CVD and liquid-phase exfoliation have enabled high-quality graphene production, their translation to mass production is hindered by high operational costs, energy demands, and limited throughput. In this context, scalable alternatives such as biomass-derived graphene synthesis, hydrothermal routes, and green chemistry approaches are gaining increasing attention due to their potential to reduce both cost and environmental impact. However, further optimization is required to achieve consistent quality and industrial-level productivity.

A major barrier in large-scale graphene production is the lack of reproducibility and precise control over material properties. Variations in precursor purity, reaction conditions, and post-processing steps often result in inconsistencies in layer number, defect density, and lateral size, which directly influence electrical conductivity and electrochemical performance. Therefore, future research should focus on the development of standardized synthesis protocols and in-line process monitoring techniques to ensure batch-to-batch uniformity. In addition, reactor engineering advancements, such as continuous flow systems and roll-to-roll manufacturing processes, are essential for achieving scalable and controllable graphene production.

Structural instability, particularly restacking of graphene sheets, remains another key challenge that reduces accessible surface area and limits ion transport in energy storage applications. To address this, future studies should prioritize the design of three-dimensional (3D) graphene architectures, including porous foams, aerogels, and hybrid nanostructures. The incorporation of heterostructures combining graphene with materials such as transition metal dichalcogenides, MXenes, or conductive polymers can further enhance mechanical stability and electrochemical performance by preventing restacking and improving charge transport pathways.

Another critical issue is the long-term operational stability of graphene-based devices. Exposure to environmental factors such as oxygen, moisture, and thermal stress can lead to oxidation and degradation of graphene, ultimately reducing device lifetime. Reported evidence remains limited and fragmented: environmental chamber testing of rGO-based electrodes at 85°C/85% RH has shown stable resistance over time, while separate aging studies report measurable loss of oxygen-containing functional groups and reduced thermal decomposition onset temperatures [104]. However, no standardized accelerated-aging framework, such as 85°C/85% RH humidity testing or electrochemical potential cycling, has been systematically applied across graphene device types, limiting cross-study comparability.

Integration of graphene into existing energy storage technologies, such as lithium-ion batteries and supercapacitors, also presents compatibility challenges related to interface engineering and electrode architecture. Future research should focus on optimizing graphene–electrode interfaces to minimize interfacial resistance and enhance ion diffusion kinetics. Binder-free electrode designs and surface chemistry modifications represent promising directions for improving integration efficiency without compromising performance.

From a broader perspective, future development should emphasize the balance between performance, scalability, and cost-effectiveness through multi-objective optimization strategies. In addition, sustainability considerations must be integrated into the design of graphene production systems. This includes the use of green solvents, energy-efficient synthesis routes, lifecycle assessment of materials, and recycling strategies for graphene-based components to minimize environmental impact.

Overall, addressing these challenges requires a coordinated effort in scalable synthesis, structural engineering, interface optimization, and sustainable manufacturing. Advancements in these areas will be crucial for bridging the gap between laboratory-scale research and the commercialization of high-performance graphene-based energy storage devices.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Graphene and its hybrid materials have demonstrated immense potential in advancing energy storage technologies, particularly in LIBs, SIBs, and SCs. The integration of graphene with metal oxides, polymers, and nanocomposites has led to significant improvements in charge storage capacity, cycling stability, rate capability, and mechanical flexibility. By enhancing ionic and electronic conductivity, graphene-based materials have successfully addressed key challenges associated with conventional electrode and electrolyte materials, making them promising candidates for next-generation energy storage systems.

In LIBs, graphene-based anodes, cathodes, and conductive additives have enabled higher capacity retention and improved cycle life. Studies on silicon-graphene and metal oxide-graphene composites have demonstrated superior electrochemical performance, with stable cycling over hundreds of charge-discharge cycles. Similarly, graphene-enhanced cathodes in SIBs, such as Na₃V₂(PO₄)₃/graphene composites, have exhibited high energy densities and improved rate performance, making them viable alternatives to LIBs for large-scale energy storage applications. Furthermore, hybrid graphene materials in solid-state batteries and flexible SCs have opened new possibilities for wearable and portable energy storage solutions. Despite these advancements, several challenges remain before graphene-based materials can be fully commercialized. Large-scale synthesis methods must be optimized to ensure cost-effective and scalable production without compromising material quality. The long-term stability of graphene-based electrodes in practical battery conditions must be further validated through extensive real-world testing. Additionally, the environmental and economic impact of graphene production should be carefully assessed to ensure sustainable implementation. Future research should focus on the development of advanced hybrid materials that combine graphene with emerging nanostructures, such as MXenes, TMDs, and covalent organic frameworks (COFs). Machine learning and AI-driven material design strategies could further accelerate the discovery of new graphene-based composites with enhanced electrochemical properties. Furthermore, scalable production of high-performance graphene-based electrodes for commercial applications might be made possible by developments in roll-to-roll processing and 3D printing.

Despite significant progress, graphene and its hybrid materials still face challenges before full-scale application in energy storage. Future research should focus on advanced hybrid architectures, combining graphene with emerging nanostructures to enhance energy density, rate capability, and stability. Sustainable, scalable synthesis—including green chemistry and 3D printing—will be key for industrial adoption. Integration with flexible, wearable, and solid-state devices, along with AI-driven material design, can accelerate the discovery of high-performance composites. Rigorous real-world testing and assessment of environmental and economic impacts are essential for commercialization. In conclusion, graphene and its hybrid materials hold transformative potential for the future of energy storage, offering solutions to critical challenges in LIBs, SIBs, and solid-state systems. It is anticipated that graphene-enhanced batteries and SCs would be essential to the shift to high-performance and sustainable energy storage options with further study and technical advancement.
